# Userlib declarations

@difference `.decls` files take the long type names as well as the short ones, for all the new types.

A `.decls` file takes the same two ways to write a type as the language, for the parameters and the return type of a function, and they can be mixed in one file: `Scale#(value#, factor#)` is the same as `Scale:Float(value:Float, factor:Float)`. The long form is available for every type: `Byte`, `UByte`, `Short`, `UShort`, `Int`, `UInt`, `Long`, `ULong`, `Half`, `Float`, `Double` and `String` (the names of the language, not case sensitive), plus `Pointer` for a bank, an object or a [Pointer](Pointers) (`memory*` is the short form) and `Void` for a function that returns nothing (the default). A Pointer can be returned, and a `Pointer` parameter is given the address of a bank when the argument is a whole number, and the address as it is when the argument is a Pointer or an object. The short form has `%`, `%%`, `#`, `##`, `$` and `*`, and a name without a type is still an `Int`. A decorated name after the closing bracket (`:"_Name@8"`) still works, and the `:` there is not confused with the one of a type, because a type comes before the bracket.

The original only had `Int`, `Float` and `String`. Numbers are passed as C types of the same size (`int8_t`, `uint16_t`, `int64_t`, `double`, ...); numbers smaller than 32 bits are sign extended or zero extended by the caller, like C compilers do. `Half` is passed as a half precision float (`_Float16`), which no test covers. `blitzcc +k` lists them like Blitz3D does: `%` for every integer type, `#` for every float type and `$` for strings (`Scale# ( value#,factor# )`, `Big% ( value% )`), so the exact size is not shown.
